b: If there’s one recipe that all cooks need to have under their belt, it’s a classic Homemade Mac and Cheese recipe. Straight-up creamy, comforting, cheesy goodness! This classic stovetop macaroni and cheese recipe is made with a simple, budget-friendly roux-based cheese sauce and plenty of seasonings that will satisfy all of your cheesy pasta cravings. It’s amazingly delicious on its own, straight off the stovetop, and I’ve included a list of fun add-ins and other ways you can make it your own.

“I have tried so many Mac and Cheese recipes and my kids haven’t liked a single one. I gave this one a try tonight and they all came back for seconds. We will definitely be adding it to our recipe book.”

For this extra cheesy homemade mac and cheese recipe, I use slightly more roux, lots of seasonings, and about 30% more cheese than I usually do in other stovetop mac and cheese recipes I’ve shared. The roux gives the sauce enough body to cling to the macaroni, and all that cheddar makes it so luxuriously creamy and cheesy that I couldn’t stop sneaking forkfuls between photographs. My favorite part? It stays smooth and creamy when I reheat the leftovers in the microwave with a splash of milk. Mac and cheese heaven! 🙌

I make the sauce while the macaroni boils, so I can get four servings on the table in 25 minutes for just under $1 each. Half a teaspoon of hot sauce brightens up the sharp cheddar without making it spicy, so it’s an easy one to serve to kids, too. If you’re making it for Thanksgiving or another holiday, you can serve it straight from the stovetop and save the oven for your mains. However, I’ve included instructions if you want to transform this into a baked mac and cheese in the recipe card below, too.

Use block cheese for the creamiest sauce. Pre-shredded cheese has a coating that keeps it from melting smoothly, which is the biggest reason mac and cheese turns grainy. Shredding it yourself using the large holes on a box grater (shown below) takes a minute but makes all the difference.

Keep the roux-to-milk ratio steady. Using 3 tablespoons each of butter and flour to 2 cups (500ml) of milk gives you a dependable base (a roux) that thickens in about 5 minutes. Heat is what activates the roux, so be patient during this step!
Add the milk slowly. I pour in a little at a time and whisk until it thickens before adding more. This quick step keeps the sauce silky and helps it thicken faster.

Turn off the heat before adding cheese. Add it by the handful and whisk until it melts. If it cools too much, warm it gently on low. Keeping it below a simmer (do not let it boil!) prevents the cheese from separating or becoming grainy.
As the noodles sit in the sauce, they will absorb and thicken it. Add a splash of milk to reach your desired consistency if needed.

Use the stovetop method for an easy win. The sauce comes together in one pot while the pasta cooks, so you can have dinner on the table in about 20-25 minutes. It’s quick, easy, and doesn’t call for any extra steps unless you want to bake it, of course!
The Best Cheeses for Mac and Cheese

Sharp cheddar is my first pick for mac and cheese. It has a strong enough flavor to come through once you stir the sauce into the macaroni, and a store-brand block (use whatever is cheapest!) keeps the cost down. I always grate it myself so it melts smoothly. If you’re comparing blocks at the store, check the price per ounce. A bigger block can be a better buy if you’ll use the rest in other meals like sandwiches or quesadillas.

However, one of the easiest ways to save money on this recipe is to start with whatever cheese is already in your fridge. Medium cheddar does work here and gives the sauce a milder flavor. If you have a little Monterey Jack, Colby, or Gouda, grate it and use it in place of some or all of the cheddar. If it makes more sense for your budget, buy a smaller block of sharp cheddar and make up any difference with the cheese you already have (you’ll need 2½ cups of grated cheese total).
I avoid processed cheese products like Kraft Singles or Velveeta in this mac and cheese recipe because I prefer the flavor of sharp cheddar in the homemade sauce.

What about Kraft Singles or Velveeta? Both are made to melt smoothly, which can be handy for a grilled cheese or a quick dip! I skip them here because I prefer to build the sauce from scratch using real, recognizable ingredients. A simple butter-and-flour roux gives me the creamy texture I want, and sharp cheddar gives the sauce a stronger cheese flavor.
If I’m buying cheese specifically for this recipe, a block of cheddar gives me something I can use in other meals, too.

Mac and cheese makes a super easy dinner when you pair it with simple dishes you can pop in the oven or slow cooker. And it’s especially delicious with anything barbecue! For BBQ pulled pork sandwiches, I toss my slow cooker pulled pork with whatever barbecue sauce I’ve got in the cupboard and pile it onto buns with dill pickles. I also like mac and cheese with fried chicken (try our air fryer fried chicken to skip the deep fryer) and green beans. It’s a classic comfort food pairing, and the air fryer leaves the stovetop free for both sides.
Shown here with a pulled pork sandwich and simple side salad.
Or try it with some crispy fried chicken and green beans.

Or if I’ve got my meatloaf in the oven, I start the mac with about 20 minutes left on the timer so it’s ready to scoop by the time the loaf has rested. I also like to add roasted broccoli for a little crunch from those browned edges! If you’re serving it with roast turkey for the holidays, you can either make the mac ahead and reheat it OR start it while the turkey rests for the creamiest texture. 😋

This incredibly creamy and cheesy homemade mac and cheese recipe features an easy cheese sauce made with sharp cheddar, milk, and butter.
Cook the macaroni according to the package directions (boil for 7-8 minutes, or until tender). Drain the macaroni in a colander and set aside.
Place the butter and flour in a medium pot over medium heat. Whisk until the butter is melted and the mixture begins to bubble. Once bubbling, continue to whisk and cook for one minute.
After cooking the butter and flour roux, slowly whisk in the milk. I added a few tablespoons at a time, letting each addition thicken before adding more milk.

Cook and whisk over medium heat until the milk gently simmers and thickens to the consistency of heavy cream, about 5 minutes. Be patient and let it fully thicken before adding the cheese, or it won’t melt smoothly.
Once it thickens, turn the burner off. Season the sauce with onion powder, garlic powder, paprika, salt, pepper, and hot sauce. Whisk to combine.

Add the shredded block cheddar a handful at a time, whisking until each addition melts before adding more. If the sauce cools too much, briefly return it to low heat, but don’t let it boil, or it may separate and turn grainy.

Add the cooked and drained pasta to the pot with the cheese sauce and stir to combine. If your pasta appears to be drowning in cheese, don’t worry! It’ll be the perfect consistency as the macaroni absorbs the sauce and thickens up.
Preheat the oven to 350ºF/180C/160C fan or Gas Mark 4.
After combining the drained pasta and cheese sauce, transfer it to a casserole dish.
Top with more shredded cheese, then bake for 15 minutes.
To achieve a golden brown crispy cheese crust, turn on the oven’s broiler for just a few short minutes, watching it closely to prevent burning.

*I use whole milk here because it’s affordable, easy to find, and adds a lovely creaminess to the sauce. The roux also thickens it just enough to coat the macaroni. Lower-fat milk could work, too, though the sauce may be a little thinner and less creamy. I haven’t tried other options, like evaporated milk, in this recipe. It’s more concentrated than whole milk, so the sauce could turn out thicker. If evaporated milk is all you’ve got, I recommend you make my skillet mac and cheese instead!

**This small amount of hot sauce does NOT make the mac and cheese spicy. It just brightens the flavor a bit and adds a little tang. I use it in place of the ground mustard you’ll find in some other mac and cheese recipes. If you’d prefer to use mustard, swap the hot sauce for ½ tsp of Dijon mustard.

***Grate your cheddar from a block. Pre-shredded cheese is usually dusted with an anti-caking powder like potato starch or cellulose (a plant fiber). That powder coats each shred so the cheese stays loose in the bag. The coating can also make the cheese melt less evenly, leaving you with a slightly grainy sauce. For the smoothest macaroni, I grate a block of sharp cheddar and whisk it in a handful at a time with the heat off. Medium cheddar works if you want a milder flavor, or you can swap the cheddar for other good melting cheeses, like Monterey Jack, Colby, or Gouda.

This classic stovetop mac and cheese recipe starts with a roux, which is a cooked mixture of flour and fat (in this case, butter). The roux thickens the sauce and helps the cheese melt smoothly into the sauce instead of clumping up as it melts. While there are ways to make a cheese sauce without a roux, taking this extra step definitely creates the creamiest, dreamiest cheese sauce for this dish.

Prep it ahead! I like this pasta best straight from the pot, but you can grate the cheese and measure the seasonings ahead to save a few minutes. If you want to make the whole dish the day before, pop it in the fridge and warm it gently (see below) with a splash of milk when you’re ready to serve.
Fridge: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for 3-4 days. The macaroni soaks up more of the sauce as it sits, so it’ll be a little thicker the next day.

Reheating: I reheat individual portions in the microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring in between, and add a splash of milk if the sauce needs loosening. For a larger portion, warm it in a saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring often and adding a little milk as needed. Keep it below a boil so the sauce stays smooth.

Freezing: I’d skip freezing this one. The sauce can turn grainy or separate when it thaws, and the macaroni can get softer. If you’re cooking for two and want fewer leftovers, you can halve the recipe.

How to Make Homemade Mac and Cheese step-by-step photos
Gather all your ingredients: Start by grating the sharp cheddar on the large holes of a box grater, so you have 2½ cups ready to go when you need it.

Cook the macaroni: Boil 8 oz. of macaroni according to the package directions (7-8 minutes, or just until tender). I like to taste an elbow before draining. It should be tender all the way through, with a little bite. Drain the macaroni in a colander and set it aside.

Start the roux: You can start the sauce while the macaroni boils, or use the same pot once the pasta is draining to save on dishes. Add 3 Tbsp butter and 3 Tbsp all-purpose flour over medium heat. Whisk as the butter melts and the flour blends into a pale paste. Once it starts bubbling and looks foamy, keep whisking for about one minute.

Whisk in the milk: Slowly whisk in 2 cups of whole milk, a few tablespoons at a time. The roux will look quite thick after those first few splashes. Keep whisking over medium heat and let each addition thicken before pouring in more. The mixture will loosen into a smooth sauce as you add the rest of the milk.

Check the thickness: Let the sauce come to a gentle simmer over medium heat, whisking often. Look for small bubbles and a sauce that coats the back of a spoon like heavy cream. This takes about 5 minutes. Once it’s thick enough to leave a light coating on the spoon (shown above), turn off the burner.

Season the sauce: Whisk in ½ tsp onion powder, ½ tsp garlic powder, ½ tsp paprika, ¾ tsp salt, ¼ tsp freshly cracked black pepper, and ½ tsp hot sauce. The paprika and hot sauce will give the pale sauce a light orange tint as you whisk them in.

Add the cheddar: With the heat off, whisk in the 2½ cups of shredded cheddar one handful at a time. Wait until you can’t see any shreds from the last handful before adding the next. If the sauce cools before all the cheese melts, put it back over low heat briefly. Keep it below a simmer so it stays smooth. Overheating cheese sauces will cause them to break and become grainy and oily.

Check the cheese sauce: Once all the cheese has melted, the sauce should look glossy and easily coat the back of a spoon (see above). You can give it a taste at this point and adjust the seasonings if you’d like. Remember, you want the sauce to be seasoned well because the flavor intensity will be diluted a bit once the macaroni is added.

Add pasta: Add the cooked and drained macaroni back to the pot and stir to combine with the cheese sauce. If your pasta appears to be drowning in cheese, don’t worry! It’ll be the perfect consistency soon as the macaroni absorbs the sauce and thickens up.
And that’s it! Don’t tell me you don’t want to dive right into that pot and swim around a bit. 😂

Here’s where the recipe can get really fun. In addition to changing the cheeses, you can switch up the herbs and spices, add in some veggies, or your favorite protein to make your own creation. Here are some other fun ingredients to add:
Proteins: Cooked chicken, bacon, sausage, tuna, ham
Vegetables: Broccoli, spinach, peas, pickled jalapeños, Rotel
Sauces & Condiments: kimchi, pesto, Sriracha, salsa, Buffalo sauce
